title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
hook: a new cricket bat gets oiled before it's played; the Charaka Samhita says something similar about a body

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine woke the senses one by one: eyes, teeth, tongue, mouth, skin.

A new cricket bat comes home, pale and smelling of fresh wood, and the first job isn't to hit anything. It's to oil it: a thin coat, rubbed in by hand, left to soak, then another. Skip it, and the wood can dry out and crack the first time a hard ball meets it. Players who care about their bats do this without being told. The Charaka Samhita makes the same kind of point, with older objects, about the human body.
screen: `A NEW BAT, OILED FIRST.` → `DRY WOOD CRACKS.` → `THE SAME POINT, ABOUT A BODY.`

segments.voice: The practice is called abhyanga: oiling and rubbing the body, a part of the classical daily round, usually before the bath. The Charaka Samhita explains it with three everyday things from its own world. Paraphrased: a clay pot, a piece of leather, the axle of a cart. Each becomes strong and holds up to use when it's oiled. So too the body, the text says: it becomes firm, its skin smooth, and it's less easily hurt by strain. The classical texts give particular care to a few places: the head, the ears, the feet. Look at the picture it chooses. The body as a well-used thing: not a temple on a shelf, not a problem to fix, but something that does work every day, carried, pressed, walked on. Things that work hard get looked after. And it's done with the hands, no machine, no specialist. It's one of the few parts of the routine where a person touches their own body slowly, all over, with care. For some people that's harder than it sounds, and that's worth noticing, gently. In some families it's done for someone else, too: a grandmother oiling a child's hair, a parent rubbing a baby's legs. Hands passing the habit down. The text frames abhyanga as health, but the gesture carries something more: the body treated as worth tending. And a plain note: oil isn't right for every skin or every condition. Like everything in the round, it's a practice to fit to a person, not a rule to force onto one.
screen: `ABHYANGA: OIL, RUBBED IN BY HAND` · `A POT, A HIDE, AN AXLE` · `A WELL-USED THING, LOOKED AFTER` · `HANDS PASSING THE HABIT DOWN`

segments.voice: No oil needed: rub your palms together until they're warm, then press slowly from wrist to elbow, then the shoulders and the back of the neck, and the soles of the feet if that's comfortable. Move as if the body were something valuable that does a lot of work, then let the hands rest. If you pray, you can give thanks for whatever part of the body carried you today.
The daily routine. Its oiling, abhyanga, treats the body like a pot, a hide or an axle: something used every day, made strong by care.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. A body that works hard is worth tending. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Ayurveda's daily round, abhyanga is a self-massage with warm oil before bathing, and in some Hindu families oiling a child's hair or a baby's body is a regular household practice.

notes: Charaka's pot, leather and axle comparison recalled from Sutrasthana 5 (verse numbers around 5.85–5.86); confirm objects and wording of the paraphrase, and the benefits listed (firmness, smooth skin, resistance to strain).
'Head, ears, feet' given particular care: confirm (Charaka has separate passages on head oil, ear oil and foot massage; Ashtanga Hridaya 2.8–9 names them).
The cricket-bat hook is an everyday analogy, not a claim about the texts; the teach says 'in some families'.
Medical caution line ('oil isn't right for every skin or every condition') is deliberate.
